name: CIELAB (L*a*b*)
description: Perceptually uniform color space derived from CIE XYZ via a cube-root-based non-linear transform. Designed so that equal numerical distances correspond to equal perceived color differences. The industry standard for color difference (ΔE) calculations.

L*.name: Perceptual Lightness
L*.notes: 0 = black, 100 = white diffuser. Perceptually linear (unlike sRGB or linear RGB).

a*.name: Green-Red axis
a*.notes: Negative = green, positive = red/magenta. Named after the opponent color process.

cylindrical_form.name: CIELCh
cylindrical_form.notes: Cylindrical form. h° is the hue angle, C* is chroma (colorfulness).

delta_e.CIEDE2000: Complex formula accounting for hue/chroma/lightness weighting — industry standard
delta_e.just_noticeable_difference: ΔE76 ≈ 1 is roughly the smallest perceptible difference
delta_e.wcag_contrast: WCAG 2.x uses relative luminance (Y from XYZ, NOT L*) — do not confuse

use_cases: Accessibility contrast checking (use relative luminance from XYZ)
Legacy perceptual color math (use OKLab for new work)

vs_oklab.advantage: Industry standard, WCAG/ISO reference, established ΔE formulas
vs_oklab.disadvantage: Hue shifts in blue region, more complex math than OKLab, worse for GLSL
vs_oklab.recommendation: Use OKLab for new generative art. Use CIELAB when interfacing with industry tools or WCAG.

art_notes: CIELAB is where the color science establishment lives. If you're doing ΔE 2000 comparisons or talking to Pantone, you're here. For generative art, OKLab is better. But understanding CIELAB gives you the vocabulary to read color science papers.
